stem: What is the purpose of a feasibility study?

options.content: To decide if the solution is worth developing
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: To test the finished program thoroughly for faults
options.rationale: Testing comes later in the cycle.

options.content: To train the users how to use the new system
options.rationale: Training happens at implementation.

options.content: To write the program code for the new system
options.rationale: Coding is part of development.

explanation: A feasibility study decides whether to go ahead with the project.

stem: Which fact-finding technique involves the analyst watching staff do their normal work?

options.rationale: Correct.
An interview is a set of questions asked face to face.
A questionnaire is a set of written questions.
That means studying forms and reports.

explanation: Observation shows what really happens.

stem: Which is a disadvantage of using a questionnaire to collect facts?

options.content: Only one person can be asked at a time
options.rationale: Many people can be asked at once.

options.content: Many questionnaires may not be returned
options.rationale: Correct: the response rate can be low.

options.content: It is the most expensive technique
options.rationale: Questionnaires are cheap.

options.content: The analyst must travel to every person
options.rationale: Questionnaires can be given out or sent.

explanation: Low response and little detail are the main disadvantages.

stem: Which is an advantage of an interview compared with a questionnaire?

options.content: A very large number of people can be asked cheaply
options.rationale: That is an advantage of questionnaires.

options.content: It never takes very much time to carry out
options.rationale: Interviews take a long time.

options.content: Questions can be explained and followed up
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: The answers can be compared automatically
options.rationale: Interview answers are harder to compare.

explanation: Interviews allow follow-up questions and detail.

stem: A company wants a system that has to hold personal details of customers. The analyst checks that the plan respects the data protection laws. Which type of feasibility is this?

options.rationale: Technical feasibility concerns the hardware, software and skills.
Correct.
Economic feasibility concerns costs and benefits.
Schedule feasibility concerns the time needed.

explanation: Checking the law is legal feasibility.
hints: Which feasibility type is about laws and regulations?

stem: The staff of a small clinic say they will not use a computer system because they prefer their paper cards. Which type of feasibility is most affected?

options.rationale: The technology may be available.
The question is about acceptance, not cost.
Nothing here concerns the law.
Correct: it concerns whether the people will accept and use the system.

explanation: Operational feasibility asks whether the users will use the system.

stem: Which is the best requirement for a user requirements specification?

options.rationale: This cannot be tested.
This cannot be tested.

options.content: The program should use modern ideas and methods
options.rationale: This is vague and cannot be tested.

options.content: A booking is saved in under 3 seconds
options.rationale: Correct: it is specific and can be tested.

explanation: A good requirement is specific and testable.
hints: Can you check the requirement with a test?

stem: Which document is produced at the end of the feasibility study?

options.rationale: That follows, in the analysis stage.
That is produced near implementation.
Correct.
The test plan is produced in design.

explanation: The study reports its findings and recommendation to the management.
hints: What does the management need to decide?

stem: Document inspection shows how staff actually carry out their work.
explanation: False. It shows the data and forms that are used, but observation shows how the work is done.

stem: Match each type of feasibility to the question it asks.

right.content: Will the users accept and use the system?
Does the system obey the law?
Can it be finished in the time allowed?
Are the hardware, software and skills available?
Do the benefits outweigh the costs?

explanation: Each type tests a different aspect.

stem: Match each fact-finding technique to the situation in which it is the best choice.

right.content: The analyst needs to see how the work is really done
The analyst needs to see which data items the forms contain
Detailed opinions are needed from a few managers
Simple views are needed from 400 customers

explanation: Choose the technique to suit the information needed.

stem: Complete the sentences about fact finding.

payload.template: A {{blank:a}} is a set of written questions given to many people. An {{blank:b}} is a face-to-face conversation with questions.

explanation: Questionnaire: written; interview: face to face.

stem: Name the document that lists what the new system must do and is agreed with the users.
explanation: The user requirements specification.

stem: A shop will pay US\$3 600 for a stock control system that saves US\$150 a month. Calculate the payback period, in months.
An analyst sends 150 questionnaires to customers and 96 are returned. Calculate the response rate as a percentage.
A system costs US\$4200 to set up and saves US\$175 a month. It costs US\$25 a month to run. Calculate the net benefit, in US\$, after 24 months. (A negative answer means a net loss.)
explanation: The net benefit is -600: after 24 months the system has not yet paid for itself.
hints: Savings over 24 months minus the cost minus the running costs.

stem: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of each of the following fact-finding techniques: interviews and questionnaires. [4]

points.description: Interview advantage: detailed answers and the analyst can ask follow-up questions
Interview disadvantage: time-consuming (and expensive) to carry out
Questionnaire advantage: many people can be asked cheaply and the answers are easy to compare
Questionnaire disadvantage: many are not returned, and they give little detail

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Interviews give detailed answers and allow follow-up questions, but they take a long time. Questionnaires can be given cheaply to many people and the answers are easy to compare, but many are not returned and the answers have little detail.

explanation: One advantage and one disadvantage for each.
hints: Name the technique, then an advantage and a disadvantage.

stem: A bus company in Gweru is considering a ticketing system. Explain what is tested in the economic, technical and operational feasibility studies. [3]

points.description: Economic: whether the benefits (savings, extra income) outweigh the costs
Technical: whether suitable hardware, software and skills are available
Operational: whether the staff and customers will accept and use the system

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Economic: whether the benefits outweigh the costs. Technical: whether the hardware, software and skills are available. Operational: whether the staff and customers will accept and use the system.

explanation: One test for each type.
hints: Technical, economic and operational are three of the types.

stem: Give three reasons why a user requirements specification is needed. [3]

points.description: It records what the system must do, agreed by the users
It gives the developers a clear target to design and build
It can be used at the end to test whether the system meets the requirements

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: It records what the users need and have agreed to. It gives the developers a clear target. It is used at the end to check that the finished system meets the requirements.

explanation: Agreement, target, test.
hints: Think about what the users and the developers need to agree.

stem: An analyst uses both observation and document inspection to study how a clinic records appointments. Explain why it is better to use both techniques than only one. [4]

points.description: Observation shows how the work is really done, including problems the staff do not mention
Document inspection shows the actual forms, data items and their formats
Observation alone does not show the data fields or the volumes of data
Document inspection alone does not show the steps of the process or the delays

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Observation shows how the work is really done and any problems staff do not mention, but does not show the data fields. Document inspection shows the forms and data items but not the steps or delays. Using both gives a complete picture.

explanation: Each technique covers what the other misses.
hints: Think about what each technique shows that the other does not.

stem: A school in Mutare is considering a fees system that costs US\$5400 and saves US\$300 a month in clerks' time. The analyst sent 200 questionnaires to parents and 138 were returned.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the payback period, in months.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the response rate to the questionnaire, as a percentage.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State two other tests of feasibility that the analyst should make, and say what each tests.

points.description: Technical: whether the equipment and skills are available (or operational: whether the staff will use it)
Legal or schedule: whether the system keeps the law about personal data (or whether it can be finished in time)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Technical feasibility tests whether the equipment and skills are available. Legal feasibility tests whether the system obeys the law about personal data.

parts.explanation: Name two types and say what they test.

explanation: Payback 5400 ÷ 300 = 18 months; response rate 138 ÷ 200 = 69%.
hints: Work out the payback and the percentages.

stem: A school in Chinhoyi wants to replace its paper-based library records with a computer system. The librarian, two teachers and 300 learners use the library.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Choose a fact-finding technique to collect the opinions of the 300 learners and give a reason.

points.description: A questionnaire
Many people can be asked cheaply and the answers can be compared

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A questionnaire, because 300 learners can be asked cheaply and the answers are easy to compare.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Choose a technique to find out in detail how the librarian lends books and give a reason.

points.description: An interview (or observation)
The librarian can describe the process in detail and the analyst can ask follow-up questions (or the analyst sees what really happens)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: An interview, because the librarian can describe the process in detail and the analyst can ask follow-up questions.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State what the analyst learns by inspecting the cards that are currently filled in when a book is borrowed.

points.description: Which data items are recorded (for example title, borrower and dates)
The layout and format of the data that the new system must hold

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The analyst learns which data items are recorded, such as the title, borrower and dates, and their format.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Give two items that should appear in the user requirements specification.

points.description: What the system must do, for example record a loan and show overdue books
A constraint, such as the budget or the time available (or the inputs and outputs required)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The system must record a loan and list overdue books, and it must cost no more than the budget.

explanation: A questionnaire reaches all 300 parents; interviews give detail; observation shows the real process.
hints: Think about when each technique is most suitable.
